messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Maren Holst is a 39-year-old city council member of Norwegian descent who has been married for eleven years and, by most external measures, occupies a position of considerable authority and visibility in her community. She came to the intake appointment dressed carefully, her composure intact until the third session, when she described for the first time what she had witnessed as a child growing up in a household where her father's violence toward her mother had been as unpredictable as it was sustained. It was that unpredictability, she explained, that had shaped everything.

The incident she returned to most often — though she could not fully reconstruct it — occurred when she was approximately nine years old. She remembered the kitchen, the overhead light, the particular pitch of her mother's voice before it changed. She remembered being pressed into the corner between the refrigerator and the wall, her knees drawn up, her body making itself small. What followed in the middle of the memory was simply gone, a blank she had tried for decades to fill. Then it resumed: her mother on the floor, a specific quality of silence, and herself still in that corner, still folded. Those two edges of the event — the moments just before and just after — were rendered in what she described as unbearable sharpness, while the center remained inaccessible. She had come to believe that whatever had happened in that gap was the part she most needed to understand, and also the part her mind had decided she could not survive knowing.

In the years since, Maren had built a life organized around the management of what she did not name as fear but which functioned as a constant environmental audit. At council meetings, she positioned herself with her back to the wall and a clear sightline to the exit. She watched her colleagues closely — not their arguments, but their hands, their jaws, the micro-shifts in their posture that might precede something she could not yet name. She was aware that this made her appear watchful and composed, which served her professionally, but she understood privately that she was scanning for something specific and ancient. When a colleague raised his voice during a budget hearing three months ago, Maren felt her body curl inward at the shoulders, her knees pressing together under the council table, her weight shifting back into her chair in a way she recognized with a cold, dissociated clarity as the posture of a nine-year-old in a kitchen corner. She had not moved from her seat. She had continued speaking. But something in her had been somewhere else entirely.

Sleep had become unreliable in a way that had worsened over the past year. She described lying awake in what she acknowledged was a safe and quiet home, beside a husband she trusted, unable to locate the source of the vigilance that kept her from crossing into sleep. She did not report nightmares so much as a refusal of unconsciousness — a sense that lowering her guard had consequences she could not rationally articulate but could not override.

Outside the council chambers, Maren's world had contracted in ways she had rationalized as preference. There were a handful of places — her office, her own kitchen, a particular coffee shop where she knew the staff — where she felt something approximating ease. Elsewhere, she was working. Her social life had quietly narrowed; her husband had remarked, gently and then less gently, that she no longer accompanied him to gatherings she once attended without apparent difficulty. She had not explained why. She was not certain she could.

What finally brought her to seek help was a constituent meeting in which a man raised his voice at her across a conference table — nothing threatening by any objective measure, a frustrated homeowner, a zoning dispute — and she had found herself unable to speak for a full thirty seconds. Her staff had noticed. She had noticed them noticing. What she most feared, she said quietly at the end of the intake, was that she was becoming smaller. What she most hoped was that the blank in the middle of that memory was not, in fact, the thing holding everything else in place.
